opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it hit me in small ways before the big ones. The first thing I noticed was the pace. People in New York walk fast, talk fast, and decide fast. Coming from an academic environment where you could spend a whole afternoon thinking through one problem, it felt like everyone around me was already three steps ahead and expected you to keep up.

The second thing was how direct people are. Back home, and even in a lot of research settings, there's a softer way of giving feedback. You hint at something and the other person understands. In New York, people just say it: "This doesn't work," or "I don't think that's a good idea." At first it felt a bit harsh, and I took some of it personally. Over time I realized it's actually very efficient, and it's not personal at all. It's just how people get things done.

Then there's the diversity. You walk down one street and hear five languages. That was exciting, but it also made me realize how much I'd been living in a fairly homogeneous bubble, both culturally and professionally. I was surrounded by people who thought about the world the way I did, through computer science and systems. In New York I'd meet people in finance, art, media, and food, all of them very ambitious and with a completely different set of values about what success means.

And of course there were the practical things: figuring out the subway, how expensive everything is, tipping culture, and how small the apartments are. Those were funny at first and then just part of life.

Looking back, I think the biggest shift was internal. The culture shock pushed me to be more assertive, to speak up earlier, and to be comfortable not having everything figured out before I act. That turned out to be really useful later, especially when it came to building things in open source and working with a lot of people very quickly.

r001.rationale: The response describes culture shock from New York’s pace, directness, diversity, and practical differences, but does not attribute it being relatively mild to feeling accepted there.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing that hit me wasn't anything big or dramatic, it was the small stuff. Like, I remember walking into a bodega the first week and the guy behind the counter just said, "What do you want?" No smile, no greeting, nothing. And in my head I was like, did I do something wrong? Back home there's this whole layer of politeness, and here it felt almost rude. But after a few months I realized that's actually New York being efficient. He wasn't being rude, he was respecting my time. Now I kind of love it.

The second thing was the pace of talking. People here interrupt each other constantly, and at first I thought I was being steamrolled in every conversation. I'd be waiting for my turn, and my turn never came. Eventually a friend told me, "Nobody is going to hand you the floor, you have to take it." That was a real adjustment, especially professionally. In meetings I had to learn to just jump in, which felt aggressive to me at the time but is completely normal here.

And then there's the food thing, which sounds trivial but it wasn't. I had this idea that New York had everything, and it does, but the Chinese food in Manhattan is mostly for people who aren't Chinese. I had to go all the way out to Flushing to find something that actually tasted like home. The first time I did that, I almost cried over a bowl of noodles. So that became my ritual, every couple of weeks, forty-five minutes on the 7 train just to feel grounded again.

But I think the deepest shock was realizing how much of my identity was tied to context I no longer had. Nobody knew who I was, what school I went to, what my family did. That's uncomfortable, but it's also freeing. You get to decide from scratch who you are. That part took longer than the bodega stuff, maybe a year or two, but it's the part I'm most grateful for.

r001.rationale: The response describes culture shock around New York’s directness, conversational pace, food, and identity. It does not attribute relatively mild culture shock to feeling accepted there.

astra-6.text: For me, the biggest culture shock was how directly people communicated. In New York, people would tell you exactly what they thought, and at first I wasn’t sure how to interpret that. Were they upset, or was that just how they talked? Gradually, I learned not to take that directness personally. I also had to get more comfortable speaking up—asking questions and saying what I wanted instead of expecting people to pick up on it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes direct communication as the biggest culture shock and learning to adapt; it does not attribute relatively mild culture shock to feeling accepted in New York.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the biggest culture shock was how direct people were. In New York, people tend to tell you what they think, and they expect you to speak up, too. At first, I sometimes interpreted that directness as impatience. Gradually, I started to appreciate it—you spend less time guessing what someone means. But learning to express my own opinions that openly took some adjustment.
